meta.title: Twelve Ways to Be Wrong About AI-Assisted Coding
meta.author: ubernostrum

comments.author: bmo
comments.text:
The author is one of the founders of Software Carpentry so he's been thinking about how to measure software productivity better since long before LLMs.

The cited METR study is really interesting but not for the most obvious reason. The headline result to a lot of people was "AI made people slower" and that can be dismissed by pointing out that it was 2025-era LLMs and they're getting better all the time, etc. The more interesting finding though is that their own estimates after the fact didn't match reality, even directionally, and there's probably something fundamental there that poses real challenges to any kind of measurement that most companies are ignoring. You can't even rely on a general feeling that the tools make people more productive - people cannot tell.

An attempted followup basically failed due to selection effects:


The primary reason is that we have observed a significant increase in developers choosing not to participate in the study because they do not wish to work without AI


Developers refusing to work without AI might mean the tools work well, or it might mean their ability to do harder tasks has completely atrophied as they increasingly rely on tools.

comments.author: epidemian
comments.text:
Ohh, that's super interesting. There's a huge difference in perception between trying out a new thing out of curiosity and being enthusiastic about it, versus being forced to use a new thing (the prototypical example being workspace-only software). But i hadn't considered that this also can affect how fast we perceive things to be.

An example that comes immediately to mind is git adoption, many moons ago. I picked git enthusiastically, and i felt it was amazingly fast compared to subversion. But now i can totally imagine that someone who started using git because they were forced to, might have had the exactly opposite experience: "what? i need to 'stage' each change that i want to commit before committing? and then i need to do something else to have my commits visible by others?? this is so slow!"

comments.author: eb
comments.text:
This is a list of common problems in an evaluation study.

It really boils down to two categories of problems: 1. Measurement and 2. Methods.

For measurement, it’s difficult to develop a good measure of what’s “good” or “desirable” in AI use. It looks like proxies what are used for human coding (e.g., lines of code, speed of coding) don’t cleanly apply to AI-assisted coding.

For methods, there are basic causal setups that are often skipped, like having a control group, or a pre/post quasi experimental setup.

Methods are usually easier to fix because the researchers can control them and can adjust their setup if needed. It’s more difficult to run experiments in a real-world scenario because it requires half of the people not to receive treatment for a long period of time. For example, you cannot really ask a team not to use AI assisted coding for a year to see if AI assisted coding improves X. This ask is even more difficult if the team feels that AI will help their work.

The measurement issue is interesting. I’m not convinced that we have good measures of what “good coding” is to begin with, but AI adoption is definitely shown the need to develop something better. Most the concerns with AI assisted coding center on long term maintainability of the code base. I wonder if there is a way to measure this issue (have the developer return to the code base after X time and ask them to do something?).

comments.author: algernon
comments.text:
I think the author forgot a very important question: "What kind of harm does using AI cause?". I think that's more fundamental than any of the others, in a large part because the harm is much easier to measure: spin up a git forge, and watch the crawlers jump on it like sharks that smell blood. Scrapers DDoSing the entire internet is a measurable problem, one that each of us who self host feel.

Is any of the alleged benefits of AI, those benefits we seem to have trouble measuring correctly, worth the very real harm the crawlers do? What if we add the energy requirements of both operating the crawlers, and serving them? The training cost? Inference cost? The need for larger and larger data centers? Are these alleged benefits of AI worth sacrificing all that?

I think this is a much more important question.

comments.author: andrewballinger
comments.text:
I agree most with the assertion that it's a mistake to measure during the novelty period.

Most people are not immediately productive when asked to include a new tool in their workflow.

It takes 3-6 months to gain any kind of mastery and that's at-risk since you might come out of that period realizing the tool is junk, or simply not for you.
